businessType: Privately held industrial equipment manufacturer, founded 1994, single founder-owner holds ~100% equity. ~$85M revenue: ~70% engineered-to-order machinery, ~30% aftermarket parts and service. ~310 employees across one main plant and two satellite service depots. ~40-year reputation, long-tenured engineering and sales relationships.
stage: Revenue $85M, roughly flat-to-low-single-digit growth (mature). EBITDA ~$11M (13% margin). Aftermarket carries higher margin (~28% gross) than new machinery (~21% gross). Net debt modest (~$8M). Order backlog ~7 months. Customer concentration: top 5 customers ~38% of revenue.
ownerGoal: Achieve a liquidity event that fairly values the business, protects the workforce and 40-year reputation, and lets the 64-year-old founder transition out of day-to-day leadership within ~18-24 months; choose between selling to a financial buyer, selling to a strategic buyer, or retaining ownership and running for cash flow.
ownerConstraints: Owner-availability constraint: Founder will not commit to an earn-out or operating role beyond ~24 months; any path depending on his continued daily leadership past that is unacceptable.

Workforce/reputation constraint: Founder places high weight on protecting the ~310 employees and the brand; an outcome that gutted the workforce or relocated the plant would be heavily discounted even at a higher price.
Succession constraint: There is no ready internal CEO successor; senior engineering and key customer relationships are concentrated in the founder and 2-3 long-tenured leaders.

Valuation/clean-books constraint: Financials are reliable but not audited to PE/strategic diligence standard; quality-of-earnings, customer-contract documentation, and aftermarket-revenue durability are not yet substantiated for a buyer.
Control/timing constraint: Founder wants a defensible valuation but will not run a rushed process that signals distress to customers, competitors, or the workforce.
immediateConcern: The 64-year-old founder wants liquidity and an orderly transition within ~18-24 months but has no internal successor and depends heavily on a few long-tenured people. He must choose a path: (A) sell to a financial/PE buyer (faster, more standardized process, but typically valued on EBITDA multiple and may require an earn-out or management retention he cannot personally provide), (B) sell to a strategic buyer (a larger manufacturer or channel that could pay a premium for synergies but may integrate/relocate and is harder to source), or (C) retain ownership and run for cash flow with a hired professional manager (preserves control and reputation but defers liquidity and concentrates the founder's wealth in an illiquid, key-person-dependent asset). The business's transferable value, the durability of its aftermarket stream, and the depth of its key-person dependence are not yet substantiated to buyer-diligence standard.
availableData: Revenue $85M (flat-to-low-single-digit growth); EBITDA ~$11M (13% margin); net debt ~$8M; backlog ~7 months
Segment margins: aftermarket ~28% gross vs new machinery ~21% gross; aftermarket ~30% of revenue
Customer concentration: top 5 customers ~38% of revenue; relationships largely held by founder and 2-3 senior leaders
Comparable transactions: industrial-equipment makers of this size sell at ~5-7x EBITDA to financial buyers; strategic buyers have paid ~7-10x for assets with durable aftermarket and clean diligence
Workforce: ~310 employees, low turnover, deep tacit process knowledge; no documented succession plan
Diligence readiness: no recent quality-of-earnings study, no audited statements, aftermarket-contract documentation incomplete
unavailableData: Substantiated quality-of-earnings: normalized EBITDA after owner add-backs, one-time items, and working-capital adjustments to buyer standard
Transferable vs key-person-dependent value: how much revenue/margin survives the founder's and senior leaders' departure, and how durable the top-5 relationships are without them
Aftermarket durability: whether the ~30% aftermarket stream is contracted/recurring or relationship-dependent and at risk in a transition
Strategic-buyer landscape: which strategics would pay a synergy premium, and whether they would preserve or relocate the plant/workforce
Owner's after-tax net proceeds and personal liquidity needs under each structure (multiple, earn-out, rollover equity, tax treatment)
timeHorizon: 18-24 months to complete a transition; ~3-6 months to choose a path and prepare for a process
riskAppetite: LOW-MEDIUM (founder wants a fair, defensible outcome and is averse to distress signaling or workforce harm; not seeking to maximize price at all costs)
